prose: Population is the denominator behind GDP per capita, CO2 emissions per capita, and life expectancy. Countries that grow rapidly in population often fall in per-capita rankings even as their total output rises. {{overlapCount}} of {{firstYear}}'s top ten remain in {{latestYear}}'s top ten: {{overlapList}}.

The single largest change at the top of the table occurred in 2021, when India overtook China to become the world's most populous country. China had held the top position since the start of the series in {{firstYear}}.

Four of the ten most populous countries are also among the ten largest economies by total GDP: the United States, China, India, and Russia. The remaining six populous countries rank lower in total output, illustrating the gap between demographic and economic size.
Inside the current top 20, the largest gain since 2000 belongs to {{gainerName}}, which moved from {{gainerRank2000Ord}} in 2000 to {{gainerLatestRankOrd}} at {{gainerValueFmt}}.

methodology: Figures are total population as published in the {{sourceLink}} (indicator SP.POP.TOTL), retrieved {{retrievedAtHuman}}. The count includes all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, based on the de facto definition of population. Rankings are computed among all countries with reported data for each year; countries with no reported value in a given year are excluded from that year's ranking. Trajectory sparklines index each country's series to its own {{firstYear}}–{{latestYear}} range and are not comparable in level across rows.
